sources.citation: Vogler, Pierre. 2017 / 2024. Contribution à la classification des langues kru (Niger-Congo). ms., HAL hal-01574391 / hal-04390526. (text held under sibling checks tepo1239, barc1235)
sources.note: 'sapo' cited once as a lexical witness (item 81 'riz'); comparative phonology treats tone registers only; no accent/stress statement for Sapo.

sources.citation: Ingemann, Frances & John Duitsman. 1976-1977. A survey of Grebo dialects in Liberia. Liberian Studies Journal 7(2): 121-131. (complete-issue PDF, Indiana University ScholarWorks; held on under sibling barc1235)
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Nothing on Sapo prosody. Bibliographic payload: (a) p.129 fn.1 -- the 1972 Krahn dialect survey (which covered 'Sapo Krahn'/Southern Krahn) appeared in a University of Liberia Journal issue that was lost in shipment from the printer, no reprint planned, so that works still to obtain is effectively unobtainable except as the 1972 WALS-congress typescript; (b) p.130 -- Ingemann 1973 'Kruan Languages in Liberia' = Mid-America Linguistic Conference Papers 1972, ed. J. H. Battle & John Schweitzer, 107-113, Stillwater: Oklahoma State University (not Univ. of Kansas as in Glottolog).

sources.citation: archive.org full-text search (page_production fts endpoint), queries: '"Sapo" stress syllable Liberia language'; '"Sapo language" tone'; '"Sapo" Krahn tone accent' (0 hits); 'Kru languages stress accent initial syllable tone' (0 hits); '"Sapo" Kru phonology vowels tones'
sources.note: Only encyclopaedia (Britannica: Kru languages tonal with downstep), travel-memoir and acronym-dictionary mentions of Sapo; no text in the IA corpus pairs Sapo with stress or accent.

sources.citation: Zogbo, Lynell Marchese. 2022. Ideophones in the Kru language family. Language in Africa 3(1): 84-143. doi:10.37892/2686-8946-2022-3-1-84-143
sources.note: No Sapo data at all; Krahn (Western) examples drawn from Sauder & Wright 2000 'Krahn Grammar' (ms.) and Sauder n.d. Krahn-English dictionary; 'stress' used only for expressive emphasis on ideophones, no word-stress statement for any Kru language.

sources.citation: Eberhard, David M., Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig (eds.). 2019. Sapo [krn]. In Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 22nd ed. Dallas: SIL International. (web entry, Internet Archive copy June 2019)
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: No phonology content: the entry has no Typology field at all (unlike e.g. Klao/Grebo entries); only names, population 58,500 (2015), location, dialects, lexical similarity 84-97% with Western We, Bible portions 1956, Latin script. Print editions 1992-2009 (archive.org full-text) likewise carry no typology note for Sapo.

sources.citation: Singler, John Victor. 2015. Memorandum on Language and Ethnicity in Liberia, prepared for Liberia's Constitution Review Committee: 'Language and Ethnicity in Liberia, a Social-Science Appraisal'. New York University. 7 pp. (PDF posted on the author's site, 2022)
sources.note: No phonology content at all (no occurrence of tone, stress, accent, pitch). Sociolinguistic memo on the dialect/language distinction and ethnic labels: Sapo counted as a separate language of the Krahn complex; pp. 5-6 discuss how the Sapo, seen as 'Bush Kru' in the 1960s-70s, asserted a separate identity after 1980 and are a separate group in the 2008 census. Useful only for identity/classification, not prosody.

sources.citation: Singler, John Victor. 1990. Linguistics and Liberian languages in the 1970's and 1980's: a bibliography. Liberian Studies Journal 15(1): 108-126. (complete issue PDF)
sources.note: none for Sapo; p.110 has only Singler's remark that 'based on certain facts about the languages' tone systems' Bassa and Dewoin are closer to the Krahn languages; the Krahn bibliography (pp.117-118) lists tone items only for other Krahn varieties (Duitsman 1985 'Testing two systems for marking tone', TILL ms; Tisher 1979 'Tchien Krahn tone', TILL ms) and no Sapo-specific description - i.e. as of 1990 no dedicated Sapo phonology existed in the Liberianist record

sources.citation: Marchese, Lynell. 1986. Tense/aspect and the development of auxiliaries in Kru languages. SIL Publications in Linguistics 78. Dallas: SIL. xii+301 pp.
sources.note: Glottolog's Glottolog's most extensive description for Sapo; contains Sapo data and an introductory section on Kru phonology/transcription (tone marking). Free PDF exists but the SIL file server returned an automated-access block by automated download; download from another network and a full-text search for stress/accent, 'stress', 'accent'.

sources.citation: Duitsman, John. 1976-77. Considerations in spelling Liberian names. Liberian Studies Journal 7(2): 133-143.
sources.note: generic: 'Tone.. is an important part of the alphabets of Liberia's indigenous languages' with diacritic conventions; no statement about Sapo, Dey, Gbii or Barclayville Grebo

sources.citation: Duitsman, John, Jana Bertkau & James Laesch. 1975. A survey of Kru dialects. Studies in African Linguistics 6(1): 77-103. (full-issue PDF/text already held under sibling check west2488)
sources.note: 'Sapo Krahn (Sikɔ̃)' appears only in lexicostatistic comparisons (Klao 78% cognate with Sapo Krahn, Tajuosohn 74%); the tone section (three level tones plus contours) describes Klao; nothing on stress for Sapo or any variety.

sources.citation: Schwab, George (ed. with additional material by George W. Harley). 1947. Tribes of the Liberian Hinterland. Papers of the Peabody Museum of American Archaeology and Ethnology 31. Cambridge MA: Peabody Museum. (archive.org item tribesofliberian00schw, scanned text)
sources.note: Appendix A 'Language' (pp. 475-482) lists 'Sapa' in the Kru group and then sketches only Mano (tone, consonant alternations, word order); nothing on Sapa/Sapo phonology, tone or accent anywhere in the book.

sources.citation: Johnston, Harry Hamilton. 1906. Liberia. Vol. II. London: Hutchinson & Co. Ch. 'The Languages of Liberia' (pp. c. 1097-1135) and ch. XXXII 'Vocabularies of Liberian and other West African languages' (pp. c. 1136 ff.), with a SIKON column ('Sikon is spoken in the Sikofa country, behind Sino in Eastern Liberia'; Kru dialect of Sikon contributed by Mr. John Gow). [Glottolog ref: Johnston 1906, listed by Glottolog as an ethnographic work/overview/wordlist, assigned to Sapo]
sources.note: No statement about Sikon/Sapo tone or accent. The only prosodic remark is the book-wide transcription key preceding the vocabularies (c. p. 1136; the scanned text): "Nasalisation is marked by ~. ' shows where the accent falls; in the absence of any mark the accent falls on the penultimate syllable." -- a compiler's marking convention applied to all columns (De, Basa, Kru, Sikon, Grebo, Padebu, Kpwesi, Buzi, Vai, Mandingo..), i.e. accent MARKS in a wordlist, not a description of the language (wordlist-only data; the multi-column scanned does not allow the Sikon forms and their accent marks to…
